title: Agent Engineering
description: From vibe coding to orchestrating agent systems — where the prompt stops working

objectives.text: Recognize from the symptoms that a task has outgrown a single prompt, and name what that symptom needs instead of a prompt
Break a task into steps and pick an executor for each: AI, AI with a tool, deterministic code/API, or a human
Explain which decisions in a pipeline's architecture protect it from failure: small steps, idempotency, separating trigger and action
Check an agent against the five blocks of production readiness and assign a problem to the right block
Write an agent specification before the code: honestly mark the gaps and tell a spec from a charter

checks.question: Your prompt gives a good result in roughly seven cases out of ten. According to the symptoms table, what do you need to add?
options: Rewrite the prompt in more detail until it starts working every time
Verification of the result and retry
Run the task on a schedule
Build an interface so that another person can run the task
checks.explain: An unstable result isn't cured by yet another wording but by verification and retry (u1, “Signs you've hit the ceiling of vibe coding”). Scheduling and an interface belong to other symptoms.

checks.question: According to the lesson, how does agent engineering differ from vibe coding?
options: Agent engineering is vibe coding with a more powerful model
Vibe coding is for people who don't write code, while agent engineering requires writing everything by hand
The only difference is the number of prompts: an agent engineer has more of them
Vibe coding is for the prototype, while agent engineering is for making several unpredictable agents work reliably in production
checks.explain: Vibe coding lowers the entry barrier and gives you a prototype. Agent engineering is the discipline of coordinating agents reliably, that is, production (u1, reflection).

checks.question: A pipeline has the step “count the exact number of items in an order.” By the logic of jagged intelligence, how should you handle it?
options: Give the model a tool (calculator, DB) or make this step code
Hand it to the model: it copes with 100,000 lines of code, so it will cope with counting
Ask the model to count twice and take the average
Remove the step from the pipeline entirely
checks.explain: Precise counting is among the things AI “drops,” and what is hard for the model doesn't match what is hard for a human. Such a step gets a tool, not more trust (u2).

checks.question: The step “check that the record isn't a duplicate” is currently done by an LLM. What does the lesson advise?
options: Keep the LLM: it understands the meaning of records better
Put a second LLM after this check for verification
Replace it with deterministic code: AI where code or an API is enough is a common source of unreliability
Hand the check to a human
checks.explain: In the decomposition table, dedup is listed as Code. The lesson directly calls AI in steps where code or an API is enough the most common source of unreliability (u2, practice).

checks.question: Under the “taste rule,” how is the work split between you and AI?
options: AI chooses what to build, and you write the code
AI does everything, you only launch it
You choose what to build and verify the result; AI writes the code and fixes what you flagged
You write the code, AI checks it
checks.explain: Execution goes to AI, while direction and verification stay with the human (u2, “Taste rule for the agent engineer”).

checks.question: Why in ENERV does an email get `AI-Ingest-Done` and lose `AI Ingest` after processing?
options: So that after a crash and restart the pipeline doesn't pick up processed emails again
So that a human can see in Gmail which emails have been read
So that Gemini knows which folder to put the file in
To save space in the mailbox
checks.explain: The labels make processing idempotent: a repeated run doesn't create duplicates (u3, “What to notice,” item 2).

checks.question: In a six-step pipeline, the fourth step failed. What does orchestration give you compared with one big prompt?
options: Nothing: the whole run is lost, just as with a single prompt
The fourth step is automatically rewritten by the model
The pipeline skips the failed step on its own and moves on
The results of steps 1–3 are kept, and the failure is localized in one place that can be checked and fixed separately
checks.explain: Small steps are tested separately, and after a failure you don't lose what came before it: this is “one thread snapping” in the loom image (u3, reflection).

checks.question: What does it give you that trigger and action are separated in ENERV?
options: The trigger fires only after the action has finished without errors
An error in the action doesn't break the trigger: it keeps polling the mailbox independently
The action can be run manually without the trigger, and that is the main goal
The separation is only there to make the diagram look nicer
checks.explain: The trigger works on its own, and a processing failure doesn't stop new emails from being received (u3, “What to notice,” item 3).

checks.question: Three days ago step 4 went wrong, and you want to see what exactly the model replied. Which of the five blocks is responsible for this?
options: Execution
Cost control
Security
Observability
checks.explain: Observability is the ability to see, after the fact, the input, output, and model of every call. Without it, in the lesson's words, “you're a blind engineer” (u4).

checks.question: The main LLM provider went down. Where does the lesson solve this problem?
options: In the prompt: ask the model to “answer even during outages”
In the infrastructure: a chain of fallback providers where the next one catches the request
Manually: wait for the provider to come back up
In the security block: change the API key
checks.explain: A provider outage is a reliability issue, and it is solved by routing at the infrastructure level, not by the wording of a prompt (u4, “Pattern: 5-fallback LLM routing”).

checks.question: A retry loop got stuck, and the number of LLM calls per day is growing manyfold. Which block does this risk belong to first of all?
options: Execution
Observability
Cost control
Security
checks.explain: The question of what the worst case will cost and what happens if the bill starts multiplying sits in the Cost block (u4, practice). Retry helps reliability, but without a ceiling it turns into a money risk.

checks.question: You are filling out the spec and don't know what the cost ceiling will be. What does the lesson advise?
options: Put `[?]` and leave the question open
Write a plausible estimate so the spec looks finished
Delete the Cost section: it can be added after launch
Put the spec aside and start writing code right away
checks.explain: The spec is written before the code and must honestly show the gaps. If a question has no answer, “the foundation isn't ready to pour” (u5).

checks.question: How does an agent's charter differ from its specification?
options: The spec describes how the agent works (triggers, nodes, storage); the charter describes who it is when it talks to a human
They are the same thing; the charter is just another name
The charter describes triggers and storage, the spec describes the agent's character
Every agent needs a charter, while only an agent that talks needs a spec
checks.explain: The spec is the “plumbing,” the agent's hands. The charter is needed by a clone that talks: it holds the frame from session to session (u5, “The clone's other half: the charter”).
